script.text: Two strong players, Joliebe with the white pieces against Mortred07, in a rated bullet game -- that's chess at breakneck speed. A Sicilian Defense, sharp and double-edged. Both sides would blunder badly here. White, in the end, blundered last and best.

White opens with the king's pawn two squares forward, and Black answers on the queenside with the Sicilian -- an asymmetrical reply, meaning the two sides immediately want different things. White develops a knight and a bishop quietly, holding back the center pawns. Black brings out both knights. Everything's level.
Over the next seventeen moves, four pieces come off the board and four real mistakes slip through -- speed punishing both players -- leaving White slightly better.

Now watch move twenty-two. White's knight steps forward to c six, and in doing so it vacates its square -- unmasking the white queen's line straight down at Black's queen, which sits undefended, a whole nine points of material hanging there. Yet the knight move itself is the error. Quietly bringing the rook to d one was stronger. Five seconds spent; the position levels out again.

Move twenty-four, and the game turns. Black plays rook to e eight, one second on the clock. Taking on c one with the rook was the move -- capture first, ask questions later. Instead, the knight on e seven sits undefended: three pawns' worth of material, hanging, meaning nothing guards it if it's taken. One hasty second, and White is better again.

The finish is clean. White's king snaps off the pawn on b four, Black lifts the rook to f seven, and then the bishop slides to c four with check. That's a skewer: the king on e six must move, and when it does, the rook behind it falls. White wins.
Ninety-five percent accuracy for Joliebe, ninety-one for Mortred07 -- high numbers for a game this messy. Both stumbled badly. But White kept finding answers, and that's what decided it.
